title: Two branches of one family
evidence: Genesis 37–39 interleaves Joseph in Egypt and Judah in Canaan. Genesis 38:1 gives a broad temporal connection, not an exact shared date.

title: Ruth within the time of the judges
evidence: Ruth 1:1 explicitly names the period of the judges. It does not identify which judge was active.

title: Israel and Judah in Ahab’s time
evidence: 1 Kings 17–18 locates Elijah under Ahab; 1 Kings 22 shows Jehoshaphat allied with Ahab. These are overlapping reign contexts, not simultaneous scenes.

title: A northern fall, a southern reign
evidence: 2 Kings 18:9–10 synchronizes Samaria’s siege with Hezekiah’s reign; the later Jerusalem crisis is a distinct event.

title: Different witnesses in exile
evidence: Daniel 1 and Ezekiel 1 locate their figures within Babylonian deportation settings. The particular visions are not synchronized to the same day.

title: Jerusalem and the Babylonian exiles
evidence: Jeremiah 29 addresses deportees while Ezekiel 1 locates the prophet among exiles. These share a broad setting, not one scene.

title: Builders and prophetic voices
evidence: Ezra 5:1–2 directly connects Haggai and Zechariah with Zerubbabel and Jeshua’s building work.

title: From creation to new creation
evidence: Genesis 1–2 and Revelation 21–22 share heaven, earth, life, and divine presence imagery. This is a literary and theological connection, not simultaneity.

title: The tree and river of life
evidence: Compare Genesis 2:9–10 with Revelation 22:1–2. The imagery links beginning and consummation.

title: Passover and Christ
evidence: 1 Corinthians 5:7 explicitly describes Christ as “our passover.” This is an interpretive connection, not the same historical event.

title: Promise and faith
evidence: Romans 4 and Galatians 3 interpret Abraham’s faith and the promise. These letters belong to a much later narrative setting.

title: Commandments and Jesus’s teaching
evidence: Matthew 5:17–48 engages the law and commandments. The sermon and Sinai are distinct settings.

title: The baptism: three narratives and a witness
evidence: Matthew 3, Mark 1, and Luke 3 narrate the baptism; John 1 gives the Baptist’s witness to the Spirit.

title: One feeding, four Gospel accounts
evidence: Matthew 14, Mark 6, Luke 9, and John 6 each describe five loaves, two fish, and five thousand men.

title: The wilderness testing
evidence: Compare Matthew 4, Mark 1, and Luke 4; Matthew and Luke order the temptations differently.

title: Four witnesses to the crucifixion
evidence: Compare the Gospel accounts side by side. Differences in time descriptions are preserved.

title: The empty tomb accounts
evidence: The accounts share the empty-tomb setting and differ in detail, selection, and narrative arrangement.

title: Kings and Isaiah: the Assyrian crisis
evidence: 2 Kings 18–19 and Isaiah 36–37 preserve parallel narratives. The corresponding passage opens below.

title: One encounter, three tellings
evidence: Acts 9 narrates the event; Acts 22 and 26 recall it within Paul’s later speeches.

title: The birth narratives
evidence: Matthew 1–2 and Luke 1–2 describe Jesus’s origins with different emphases. Their details are not forced into an exact harmony.

title: Saul’s death: Samuel and Chronicles
evidence: 1 Samuel 31 and 1 Chronicles 10 recount Saul’s death at Gilboa and the actions of the people of Jabesh-gilead. Chronicles adds an editorial explanation in 10:13–14. These are accounts of one episode.
